idiom_name: std::atomic<bool> feature registry read at the toggle point
implementation_notes: A small registry of std::atomic<bool> replaces the toggle-router class: the toggle point is an ordinary if on a load(), and configuration loading stores the value once at start-up (and again on reload) with a memory order of relaxed where the flag only selects a path. std::atomic_flag is the guaranteed-lock-free alternative when only test/set semantics are needed, and feature-test macros such as __cpp_lib_atomic_wait let the code degrade gracefully on pre-C++20 toolchains. The classic runtime router is still justified when the decision needs request context (user targeting, percentage rollout) instead of a process-wide boolean, and the compile-time form below is preferable when the disabled code must not even be compiled.
pitfalls: std::memory_order_relaxed selects a path safely, but it does not publish initialised data: when the flag guards a lazily built structure, use release/acquire (or std::call_once).
std::atomic is neither copyable nor movable, so flags cannot live inside value types that get copied; keep them in one registry object or as statics.
A registry of atomics read by every request can become a contention point if flips are frequent; the flag read itself is cheap, the reload path must be rare.

variants.name: Compile-time toggle with if constexpr and build flags
variants.idiom_name: if constexpr (C++17) over a build-flag constant
variants.implementation_notes: Build-time selection in the shape modern C++ prefers: a constexpr constant set from a build flag (or a template parameter) and if constexpr (C++17) or template specialisation choosing the branch, so the discarded path is not even instantiated and no runtime state exists. Use it for optional integrations, platform variants and pay-for-what-you-use code where the feature must not ship; it is not a substitute for the pattern's runtime promise, because every flag change means a new build and a new round of testing.
pitfalls: if constexpr discards the other branch, so it must still be syntactically valid and cannot name undeclared entities; templated helpers are the way to keep a discarded branch well-formed.
Each build-flag combination is a separate binary to test and ship: do not present it as a configuration change.
